name: Glass hair
tagline: A guide to getting coils as smooth and light-catching as they can get.
image_alt: A woman in profile with a smooth, glossy braided low bun and defined edges, blowing a pink bubble.
description: What shine actually is on coily hair, a twelve-week rotation of moisture, strength and gloss treatments, and what to look for on a label.
intro: Shine is a surface effect. Smooth cuticles reflect light; rough ones scatter it. The aim is not glass hair at any cost. It is the glossiest your coils can get, with healthy hair as the part that does not move.

causes.title: What shine actually is
causes.intro: Worth being clear about this before you spend money, because a lot of shine marketing is selling something coily hair cannot do.
items: A cuticle that lies flat reflects light in one direction, so you see a highlight. A lifted or chipped one scatters it, so the hair reads dull.
Almost everything sold as a shine product is doing a single job: making the outside of the strand smoother.
Every bend in a coil turns the strand a different way, so the light leaving it goes in many directions at once.

That is why coily hair will not look like glass the way pin-straight hair can, however good the routine. What it can look like is its own best version: juicy, wet-looking, catching light along the length.
Softness has more than one source
Water keeps a strand flexible. Conditioning agents cut friction and improve how the surface feels. Lipids and film formers help smooth and protect the outside.
These are related, but they are not the same thing. Hair can feel soft from conditioning and still be damaged underneath, so the plan checks for breakage too.
Buildup reads as dull, not shiny
Past a certain point more product stops adding shine and starts adding a film.
Adding more layers is the most common reason a shine routine stops working, and clarifying is the usual fix.
Snapped ends sticking out along the length catch light at every angle.
Reducing breakage does as much for how shiny hair looks as anything you put on top of it.

stock.title: Before you start
stock.intro: Write these down today, in daylight, with photos. Check the same list at week 4, week 8 and week 12. Shine is hard to judge from memory.
items: Same spot, same time of day, same light. Indoor light hides the thing you are trying to measure.
Run a section through your fingers. Rough, squeaky, soft, waxy?
Colour, bleach, relaxer, regular heat? This decides whether the protein and bond weeks apply to you.
Does hair snap while you detangle? Do you see short broken pieces after a wash day?
Ends only, or all the way up?
Day one, or still there on day four?
What is in your rotation now
Every product you used in the last month. You will be cutting from this list, not only adding.

routine.title: Your routine
routine.intro: One wash day a week. Only the treatment step changes from week to week; everything around it stays the same.

wash.title: Your wash day
steps: Split into four to eight sections. Work a slippery conditioner or pre-wash treatment through the mid-lengths and ends, then detangle from the ends upward and twist each section as you finish it.

Shampoo onto the scalp, massage with fingertips, let the lather rinse down the lengths. Repeat only if there is real buildup. Some people need a clarifying wash every few weeks and some need it far less often. Use it when hair feels coated or dull, not by the calendar.
Moisture, ceramide, protein, bond or gloss, depending on the week. The twelve-week rotation says which. Follow its own label for timing, and if a treatment has two steps, do both.
If your treatment was not also a conditioner, finish with a slippery one and do your final detangle while the slip is there.
Section by section, while it is still dripping. Enough for slip and softness, not enough to feel coated.
Cream if you want it, then gel or mousse. Smooth each section rather than raking repeatedly.
Air-dry or diffuse low. Leave it alone while it dries. Once it is fully dry, scrunch out the cast and put one or two drops of serum or light oil over the outside and the ends.

between.title: Between wash days
groups: Check the ends, not the roots. Ends dry out first.
If they feel soft, do nothing at all.
A light mist of water and a little leave-in on the dry parts only.
Smooth with wet hands rather than raking through.
Water, a little leave-in or refresher, a touch of gel on the frizzy sections.
Let it dry undisturbed. Touching it while it dries is what causes frizz.
Resist adding butter, cream, oil, gel and mousse on top of each other.
Loose twists, braids or a pineapple. Nothing tight.
Satin bonnet or a satin pillowcase.
Keep the ends tucked away where you can.
No gloss treatment survives seven nights of friction against cotton.

rota.title: Twelve weeks
rota.intro: One treatment per wash day. This is a rotation, not a stack: it never asks you to do two of these in the same week.
phases: Get cleansing and conditioning consistent, bring in ceramides, and find out how your hair answers protein before you commit to it.
Add protein or bond treatments only if week 1 to 4 showed you need them, and start the gloss rotation.
Settle the balance you have found, keep the gloss going, and start cutting products you have proved you do not need.
items: Set the baseline. Note how long softness lasts.
First shine step. Photograph in daylight before and after.
Only if the checks in week 1 to 4 pointed to it. Skip it if your hair is strong and breaking little.
Colour, bleach, heat or visible breakage. Otherwise skip.
Second shine step. Compare with your week 4 photo.
Final polish, then your week 12 photo.
rota.note: If your hair is severely damaged or chemically processed, you may need a repair plan built around you. A twelve-week calendar is not a replacement for a stylist looking at substantial breakage.

use.title: What to use
use.intro: Products by the job they do in this plan. You do not need one of everything. Six is enough for a very good shine routine: a gentle shampoo, a clarifying or chelating shampoo for when you need it, one moisturising conditioner or mask, one leave-in, one gel, and one finishing serum. Everything else is optional.
items: Your weekly wash. Takes off sweat and light buildup without stripping what you put in last week.
Resets the surface by lifting product residue and oils. Gloss and shine products cannot work through a film of old product.
When hair feels coated, not by the calendar
For mineral deposits from hard water, which clarifying shampoos do not always remove. Some products do both jobs.
When water is hard and hair looks dull
The backbone. Softness, slip and elasticity, which is most of what makes a strand sit smooth.
Lipid support for the cuticle. The step that most changes how rough or smooth hair feels to your hand. It does not replace a rinse-out or deep conditioner.
Temporary reinforcement for damaged areas, only if your hair asked for it. If the product comes in two steps, do both, then follow with a conditioner.
Works on the inside of the fibre rather than the surface. For colour, bleach, heat or visible breakage.
The shine step. A cosmetic smoothing treatment, not a rebuild. Pick one from the shortlist below.
Slip and softness on soaking hair, before any styler.
Holds each coil in one shape while it dries. A clumped coil reflects light; a fluffed one scatters it.
One or two drops on fully dry hair. This is the polish step, and the easiest one to overdo. A dimethicone-based serum is a finish, not a conditioner.
Only if you diffuse or use hot tools.

choose.title: One gloss, not three
choose.intro: Gloss treatments are the part of this plan people get wrong, usually by buying three and using them all on the same day. Here is how to think about it.
items: Pick a single gloss and use it on weeks 4, 8 and 12. Three treatments is enough to tell whether it does anything for you, and one product at a time is the only way to know which one worked.
Several gloss and lamination treatments are acidic, and some are also conditioning masks. Follow each product's own instructions, and do not use two on the same wash day.
A gloss smooths and coats. It does not rebuild the inside of the strand, and it washes out. That is not a criticism, it is what the category is: the effect is real and it is temporary.
The cheapest gloss is a clean strand
A clarified, well-conditioned, well-clumped coil with two drops of oil on it will out-shine a glossed strand covered in four other products. Do the free part first.

shortlist.title: The shortlist
items: JVN Revive Rapid Repair Bond Gloss
Gisou Honey Gloss Ceramide Therapy Mask

ing.title: What to look for on a label
ing.intro: These are the ingredient groups this plan leans on. Hover any name to see what it is, or follow it through to its page.
items: They pull water in and hold on to it. How well that works depends on the formula and the weather.
The waxy, softening kind, not the drying kind. They are what make a conditioner feel creamy and give it slip.
Positively charged, so they stick to the damaged spots on a strand and smooth them down.
Support for the lipid layer between cuticle cells. The step that most changes how rough or smooth hair feels to your hand.
Temporary patches over damaged areas. More is not better, and too much reads as stiffness.
Short amino-acid chains, named -peptide. A different thing from a hydrolysed protein, doing a different job.
The surface smoothing most finishing serums are built on. There are four kinds and they do not behave alike.
They hold the coil clumped while it dries, which is where most definition comes from.

trouble.title: If something feels off
items: You have buildup. Clarify, then rebuild with fewer products than before and add back one at a time.
Stiff, rough or snapping after a treatment
That reads like too much protein. Stop protein treatments, condition for a few washes, and start again later with a longer gap.

Think about your history first: bleach, relaxer, heat. If that fits, try one protein or bond treatment, then condition, and see how it feels after a few washes. Stretchy hair on its own does not mean it needs protein.
Shiny on day one, dull by day three
Look at nights first. Satin, loose styles, ends tucked. Then look at how much you are touching it.
Too much oil, or oil on hair that was not dry yet. One or two drops, on fully dry hair, on the outside only.
Check that you clarified first, and that you are judging it in daylight against your own photo rather than against someone else's hair.

end.title: At the end of twelve weeks
notes: Put your week 12 daylight photo next to your week 1 one. That comparison is the only honest answer to whether this worked, and it is why the plan asks for photos on day one.

Keep the cleansing, the conditioning and the nights. Keep the gloss at whatever interval you actually enjoy. Then start cutting: anything you cannot point to a reason for is a product you are paying for and your hair is wearing for nothing.

techniques.title: The shine techniques
techniques.intro: Most of what makes coils look glossy is how they are styled, not what they are coated in. A clumped coil gives one long highlight. A cloud of separate strands gives a hundred small ones.
items: Four to eight sections, more if your hair is dense.
Smaller sections spread product evenly and cut the urge to rake through the same hair again and again.
Start with soaking wet hair. Leave-in in small sections, then smooth gel over each section with praying hands. Use your fingers or a suitable curl brush to group the coils, then stop touching them.
Raking after the coils have clumped breaks them back apart.
Smoothing the gel on with a little tension gives a sleeker result. Praying hands, finger smoothing or a styling brush all work.
Never pull hard, especially around the hairline.
Low or medium airflow, moderate heat, and leave the coils alone while they dry. Finish with cool air if you like. Be fully dry before you sleep.
Finish with a serum, if you want one
Leave-in on wet hair, then gel or mousse, then dry completely. Scrunch out the cast. One or two drops of serum on the outside and the ends.
The serum is a finish. It is not a replacement for conditioning.
Satin bonnet or pillowcase, loose twists, ends tucked in. No tight pineapple.
Hair should not have to fight cotton bedding every night.

strength.title: Three kinds of strengthening
strength.intro: Protein, amino-acid and bond-building treatments are often sold as the same thing. They are not interchangeable.
items: Hydrolysed proteins that cling to the strand and can fill in damaged spots for a while.
They suit hair that is weak, breaking and has a damage history. Too much leaves hair stiff and rough.
Smaller building blocks, often paired with conditioning.
Sold as gentler than protein. How hair responds is individual, so judge by your own results.
Formulas that claim to work on the chemistry inside the fibre, which differs by brand.
For colour, bleach, heat or visible breakage. Not a routine step for hair that is not damaged.
How to tell what your hair needs
Look at several things together: breakage while detangling, hair that feels weak when wet, a history of bleach, relaxer or heat, and how hair feels after a treatment.
Stronger-feeling after a treatment is a good sign. Stiff and rough means back off. A wet stretch test alone is not reliable, because wet hair naturally stretches.

climate.title: Water and weather
climate.intro: A good routine can still look dull if the water or the air is working against it.
items: Minerals can leave deposits that make hair look dull and feel rough. A chelating shampoo targets those. A clarifying shampoo targets product and oil. Some products do both, and you do not automatically need two.
Humectants such as glycerin pull water from the air, and hair can swell and frizz. A good gel or film former holds the coil clumped.
How well a humectant performs depends on the whole formula and the weather.
Lean on conditioning and a suitable leave-in rather than more humectants.
Lighter products may feel better, and you may need fewer layers.
